Simulation: Comparing Single-Ordering Recovery

Ziang Zhang

Question and design

How well do MPCurve, principal curves, GPLVM and Bayesian GPLVM recover one sample ordering when they share a one-dimensional initialization? We compare 30 independent random B-spline realizations under two noise levels, with 200 samples, first with 12 features and then with 50 features in a paired extension. We first compare a shared PCA start, then replace it with a shared Isomap start on the same observed data. The initial 12-feature experiment extends the earlier diagnostic of one selected trajectory to a replicated comparison. At 12 features, the four fitted methods have similar mean recovery, with large variation across trajectories. Principal curves sometimes recover a folded ordering but also show larger gains and losses. We measure recovery using absolute Spearman correlation; values near one indicate recovery up to an arbitrary reversal of the ordering.

The initial 12-feature experiment draws sample positions independently from Uniform(0,1). Its 12 feature trajectories have independent standard-normal coefficients in an eight-dimensional cubic B-spline basis, with interior knots at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 and boundary knots at 0 and 1. All features share the same sample position. The trajectories are centered over a 2,001-point uniform grid and scaled together to average signal variance one. This preserves variation in feature amplitude. No trajectory is constrained to be monotone.

Gaussian noise has standard deviation 0.25 or 1, giving average variance SNR 16 and 1. The two noise conditions share the underlying curve, sample positions and standard-normal errors within each replicate. Replicates are independent. Each method receives the same column-centered matrix, without feature variance standardization. Every generated dataset is included. Figure 1 shows the first replicate.

Figure 1. The first replicate, selected by index before fitting: all 12 generating trajectories (left) and the observed data projected onto their first two principal components at low and high noise (center and right). Color in the PCA panels denotes true sample position. Each noise condition has its own PCA computed from its observed matrix.

Common initialization and methods

PC1 is computed once from each observed matrix and supplied to every method. GPLVM and Bayesian GPLVM receive its centered coordinates scaled to variance one; this bypasses GPy’s different native PCA preprocessing. Principal curves receive the geometric PC1 line and start with exactly the same ranks. MPCurve maps PC1 ranks into 50 ordered quantile bins, introducing ties within bins. Thus the methods share the same initial direction while using their required internal representations. The initial PCA baseline makes subsequent improvement visible.

MPCurve uses the frozen MPCurver 0.3.4 implementation from the pilot: a single ordering, an RW2 smoothness prior, learned feature-specific noise and smoothness, and adaptive position weights. CAVI stops at relative ELBO tolerance \(10^{-6}\) or 2,000 sweeps. Principal curves use princurve 2.1.6 with the default df=5 smoothing splines and endpoint stretch 2; the tighter pilot stopping rule allows 1,000 iterations with relative projection-distance tolerance \(10^{-6}\).

GPy 1.13.2 supplies one-dimensional GPLVM with its native RBF plus bias covariance and Bayesian GPLVM with its native RBF covariance and 50 inducing points. Both receive one PCA start per dataset. Bayesian latent variances and inducing-point selection use a recorded replicate-specific seed. Both GP methods learn their noise and covariance parameters and use L-BFGS-B, allowing up to three blocks of 2,000 evaluations; another block is used only after an evaluation-limit stop. All settings were fixed before the first timing run. The stopping rules differ across methods, so convergence is assessed within each method’s own objective.

Ordering recovery

The first comparison uses \(P=12\) features (Figure 2 and Table 1).

Numbers above boxes are medians. The dashed horizontal line marks 0.95 recovery and the dotted line marks 0.5. A global reversal is treated as equivalent.

At low noise, median recovery is 0.612 for MPCurve, 0.526 for principal curves, 0.632 for GPLVM, and 0.615 for Bayesian GPLVM, compared with 0.620 for the initial PCA. At high noise, the corresponding medians are 0.550, 0.495, 0.566, and 0.554; initial PCA gives 0.552.

MPCurve meets its stopping rule in 60/60 fits, principal curves in 42/60, GPLVM in 60/60 and Bayesian GPLVM in 59/60. The 18 principal-curve exceptions reach the iteration cap; the one Bayesian GPLVM exception terminates with a line-search error. All finite endpoints remain in the summaries. A converged fit can still recover the wrong ordering, and a budget-limited result is an algorithmic endpoint rather than a demonstrated optimum.

Increasing feature count to 50

We extend each replicate to \(P=50\) while keeping \(N=200\), both noise levels, and all fitting settings fixed. Each extension preserves the original sample positions, the 12 original spline coefficient sets, and their standardized noise draws, then adds 38 independent features. The entire 50-feature signal is normalized to average variance one, preserving SNR 16 and 1. This common rescaling also changes the amplitudes of the original 12 signals. PCA is recomputed from all 50 observed features and shared across methods (Figure 4 and Table 3).

Figure 4. Ordering recovery with 50 features, 200 samples and 30 replicates per noise condition. Absolute Spearman correlation allows a global reversal. Boxes, whiskers and reference lines follow Figure 2; numbers above boxes are medians. Every finite endpoint is retained. Crosses indicate that the fitting stopping rule was not met.

Figure 5. Within-replicate changes in absolute Spearman recovery after extending from 12 to 50 features. Positive values favor 50 features; the dashed line marks no change. Boxes and whiskers use the Figure 2 convention. A cross indicates that either feature-count fit did not meet its stopping rule. The PCA column shows how the initial ordering itself changes when using the additional features.

At \(P=50\), MPCurve meets its stopping rule in 60/60 fits, principal curves in 52/60, GPLVM in 60/60 and Bayesian GPLVM in 59/60. Eight principal-curve fits reach the iteration cap, and one low-noise Bayesian GPLVM fit ends with a line-search error. All 60 datasets and all finite endpoints contribute to the comparison.

Increasing the feature count raises median recovery for MPCurve from 0.612 to 0.693 at low noise and from 0.550 to 0.707 at high noise (Figure 5). Both GPLVM variants also improve relative to their 12-feature medians. Initial PCA improves from 0.620 to 0.698 and from 0.552 to 0.695, respectively, so much of the change is already present at initialization. Median gains beyond the P=50 PCA baseline are only about 0.01–0.04 for MPCurve and the GP methods.

Principal curves have a wider spread: nine low-noise and eight high-noise endpoints reach at least 0.95 recovery, but their median recovery is 0.496 and 0.568. Compared with P=50 initial PCA, they lose more than 0.05 in 16/30 replicates at each noise level. Occasional near-perfect recovery coexists with substantial deterioration on other trajectories. At P=50, the paired mean principal-curve minus MPCurve difference is -0.083 (Monte Carlo SE 0.043) at low noise and -0.057 (SE 0.038) at high noise. The two GP comparators differ from MPCurve by +0.014 and +0.020 at low noise, and -0.011 and -0.002 at high noise. These are descriptive comparisons within this generator and fixed settings.

Low (SNR 16) GPLVM 2.93 2.53 0.78

Timing (Table 4) includes model setup and optimization, excluding shared simulation and PCA computation. The R timing also includes a zero-iteration fit that records the initial state; the GP timing includes its parameter archive write. Each fit uses one BLAS thread. Four fits can run concurrently: the original study used one R process and three GP workers, and the extension uses two of each. These are descriptive end-to-end measurements under each method’s stopping criterion. MPCurve remains fastest at low noise (0.26 seconds median), while GPLVM is fastest at high noise (0.64 seconds, compared with MPCurve’s 1.22 seconds). GPLVM’s high-noise median evaluation count falls from 430 to 152 when extending to 50 features, which helps explain its shorter time despite the additional features. An increase in feature count can change both work per iteration and the number of iterations, so the observed ratios are not isolated computational-complexity measurements.

Common Isomap initialization

We rerun all four methods on the same 120 observed datasets using Isomap with \(k=15\) neighbors, the package default and the earlier pilot setting. The undirected union of Euclidean nearest-neighbor edges defines shortest-path geodesic distances; all 200 samples serve as landmarks for one-dimensional classical MDS. Every graph is connected, and all samples are retained. The coordinate is centered and scaled to variance one before use. Neighborhood size is fixed across replicates and is not selected using recovery.

MPCurve maps the shared coordinate into 50 quantile bins. The two GP models receive that coordinate directly, with the same random seeds and other fitting settings as their PCA runs. Principal curves first smooth each feature against Isomap using df=5, then project observations onto the resulting geometric curve. This projection can change the actual initial ordering; Table 6 documents its effect. Thus the comparison uses a common upstream Isomap start, with each method’s required internal representation.

Figure 7. Paired change in absolute Spearman recovery after replacing PCA with Isomap initialization on the same data. Positive values favor Isomap; the dashed line marks no change. The first column compares the embeddings themselves, and the other columns compare fitted endpoints. Boxes and whiskers follow Figure 6. Crosses indicate that either the PCA or the Isomap fit did not meet its stopping rule; a triangle marks a numerical smoothing warning. Each panel contains 30 paired replicates.

Isomap substantially improves low-noise recovery (Figures 6 and 7, Table 5): for MPCurve, median absolute Spearman rises from 0.612 to 0.881 at \(P=12\) and from 0.693 to 0.9997 at \(P=50\). The other methods improve as well. At \(P=50\) and low noise, all four fitted medians are approximately 0.9997, but the number of endpoints at or above 0.95 is 24/30 for MPCurve, 29/30 for principal curves, 24/30 for GPLVM and 28/30 for Bayesian GPLVM. The corresponding means are 0.9721, 0.9957, 0.9766 and 0.9841. Principal curves therefore improve the lower tail in this condition: their paired mean advantage over MPCurve is 0.0235 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0082), despite near-identical medians.

At high noise, MPCurve has the largest median among the four methods at \(P=12\) (0.636 versus 0.550, 0.605 and 0.543). At \(P=50\), principal curves have the largest median (0.883), followed by Bayesian GPLVM (0.857), GPLVM (0.846) and MPCurve (0.839). However, principal curves’ mean recovery in this condition is 0.803, below MPCurve’s 0.834, because several replicates deteriorate substantially. The higher median does not imply better performance throughout the distribution.

All 480 fitted endpoints are finite. MPCurve and GPLVM meet their stopping rules in 120/120 fits each, principal curves in 104/120 and Bayesian GPLVM in 115/120. The exceptions are 16 principal-curve iteration caps and five Bayesian line-search errors; all remain in the analysis. One converged principal-curve fit (\(P=12\), low noise, replicate 22) emits smoothing warnings and falls back to reported df=1 within the numerical smoother despite the requested df=5. It is retained and flagged with a triangle in the figures.

With initialization cost included (Table 7), median MPCurve time is 0.22/0.52 seconds at \(P=12\) and 0.51/1.42 seconds at \(P=50\) (low/high noise). MPCurve is fastest in three conditions; at \(P=50\) and high noise, GPLVM is faster at 0.76 seconds total. The shared Isomap computation takes a median 0.04–0.08 seconds per dataset.

Interpretation and reproduction

The same-data Isomap comparison shows that initialization choice materially changes ordering recovery, especially at low noise. A good common initialization brings the typical fit close to perfect recovery at \(P=50\), while the remaining hard replicates expose differences that medians alone conceal. The relative performance depends on noise and feature count; these results describe fixed \(k=15\), not a search over Isomap neighborhoods.

At \(P=12\), the paired mean differences relative to MPCurve range from about -0.014 to +0.010, and each is smaller in magnitude than its Monte Carlo standard error. These 30 replicates therefore do not establish a consistent recovery advantage for any comparator. This is not an equivalence result. Principal curves have three low-noise endpoints above 0.95 recovery, whereas the other methods have none, but principal curves also lose more than 0.05 relative to PCA in 12/30 low-noise replicates, as often as they gain more than 0.05. Their occasional large recoveries do not translate into a higher mean or median here.

Under PCA initialization, MPCurve and both GPLVM variants usually change initial recovery only modestly. Poor recovery persists even at low noise in many replicates, motivating the Isomap comparison above. That comparison demonstrates a benefit of changing initialization without establishing it as the sole cause of every failure.

This experiment measures recovery for random cubic B-spline curves at one sample size and two feature counts under shared PCA and Isomap starts. The per-replicate results and paired differences should guide interpretation alongside the medians: a method can improve some trajectories while worsening others. These results characterize this generator and these fixed fitting settings; sensitivity to spline complexity and other neighborhood choices remains a separate question. Because PCA is recomputed at each feature count, the paired extension combines changes in the initial ordering with changes in how the methods use additional features.

The experiment directory contains generating coefficients and noise, full R fits, GP parameters and optimizer statuses, sample positions, input hashes, seeds, package versions, and plotting scripts. The reproduction instructions specify the frozen MPCurver source commit 15f2b0bbe5dfa61cd46da5160b2bc251e75a0475 and pinned comparator versions. The Isomap comparison retains the unchanged input hashes, full geodesic matrices, actual initial positions, fit records and paired PCA endpoints. The 50-feature extension also saves parent input hashes and verifies its retained coefficients and noise. Checks reconstruct every observed matrix, verify the shared PCA ranks and ordered MPCurve bins, and recompute ordering metrics from saved coordinates. The page loads saved results and performs no model fitting.
